title: Timelines (T1–T5)
text:
Comparative time-series on the year dimension (2010–2025; 2026 partial, dropped). Each standalone, companion finish.

Discipline notes: Income-comparative ones (T1, T2) use single-country extracted geography with known income. T3 uses country_universe denominators per income group. T5 is abstract-only proxy (screening corpus, 100%), “not reported ≠ not done”.





T1 — Equity Over Time


<span class="figure-badge badge-timeline">Timeline</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-equity-time.R</span>


LMIC share of annual single-country output vs their burden share (2010–2025).


Rose 16% → 36% (2010→2025) — real progress, yet still far below 83% LMIC burden share (dashed line). Shaded band = distance to reference.





T2 — QALY-Metric Convergence by Income


<span class="figure-badge badge-timeline">Timeline</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-qaly-time.R</span>


QALY use by income group over time. The metric gap over time.


LMIC 15% → 49% vs HIC 51% → 59% (2010→2025). Gap narrowed ~10pp but persists — LMIC catching up on comparable metric adoption.





T3 — Reach Over Time


<span class="figure-badge badge-timeline">Timeline</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-reach-time.R</span>


Cumulative % of each income group’s countries with ≥1 evaluation. Country universe denominators per income group.


HIC covered early; LIC reached last (28% → 96%). Geographic reach expanding but uneven — LIC coverage only recently approaching saturation.





T4 — Method Streamgraph


<span class="figure-badge badge-timeline">Timeline</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-method-stream.R</span>


Econ-eval-type composition over time (2010–2025). Stacked streamgraph.


Cost-utility 45% → 54%, cost-effectiveness 34% → 25%. Field increasingly adopts CUA (QALY) methods; CEA declining. Mirrors C11/T2 metric shift.





T5 — Decision-Usefulness Over Time


<span class="figure-badge badge-timeline">Timeline</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-decision-time.R</span>


Share of abstracts foregrounding each decision-analytic element by year. Abstract-only proxy (screening corpus, 100%).


All four rose: threshold most (12%→29%), ICER (25%→48%), PSA (15%→38%), perspective (18%→42%). Reporting improving but majority still foregrounds none.

title: HEE Research Landscape
text:
Data Quality Notes
All figures reflect audited, corrected data as of 2026-09-08:

✅ Income classification: World Bank API (fixed 30% Natural Earth error rate)
✅ Population: World Bank 2025 (fixed up to 93% underestimation for fast-growing countries)
✅ CUA/CEA harmonisation: QALY/DALY outcomes → Cost-utility (per extraction rule)
✅ DOI de-duplication: 200 duplicate DOIs removed
⚠️ Geography: Extracted-only for income figures (affiliation proxy is income-biased — see DATA_QUALITY_AUDIT.md)
⚠️ MeSH coverage: 63% C-tree, 57% E-tree, 62% N-tree (harvest 2020–2026 only; 2010–2019 harvest running)

title: Map Atlas (M1–M9)
text:
A cartographic collection sharing R/map-base.R (eligible-only counts, World Bank population, GBD 2023 burden, extracted geography, Robinson projection — discipline set by 2026-09-07 audit).

Discipline notes: Share maps (M4–M8) show only countries with ≥5 studies (grey below); M1–M3 include every country with a GBD burden row so blanks are visible; M2’s dark-purple corner = high-on-both (big countries), not missing data; M9 shades absolute counts (log) — disease contrast is the point.





M1 — Research Intensity vs Burden


<span class="figure-badge badge-atlas">Atlas</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-map-burden.R</span>


Studies per 100,000 DALYs per country, diverging around global median. Map form of Figure 7.


Blue = more research per burden than typical; red = less. Grey = no eligible study or no GBD row. 20 countries carry burden but have zero studies.





M2 — Burden × Evidence Bivariate


<span class="figure-badge badge-atlas">Atlas</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-map-bivariate.R</span>


Bivariate choropleth: high-burden/low-evidence lights up. Two-dimensional gap map.


Dark purple = high burden + high evidence (big countries); red = high burden + low evidence (the gap); blue = low burden + high evidence. Visualizes the joint distribution.





M3 — Evidence Deserts


<span class="figure-badge badge-atlas">Atlas</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-map-deserts.R</span>


0 / 1–5 / 6–20 / 21+ studies. 20 countries with burden but zero eligible studies.


The starkest map: countries with real disease burden but zero economic evaluations. Immediate priority list for evidence generation.





M4 — Who Studies Whom (Local Authorship Share)


<span class="figure-badge badge-atlas">Atlas</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-map-authorship.R</span>


Share of studies with a local author. Parachute research visible on the map. Countries with ≥5 studies only.


Low local-authorship share = parachute research. Maps the C18 finding geographically.





M5 — Model-Based vs Measured


<span class="figure-badge badge-atlas">Atlas</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-map-model.R</span>


Model-based share by country. LMIC lean on models. Countries with ≥5 studies only.


LMIC countries show higher model-dependency — consistent with C12/T4. Model-based evidence dominates where primary data is scarce.





M6 — Open Access by Country


<span class="figure-badge badge-atlas">Atlas</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-map-openaccess.R</span>


OA share by country. Countries with ≥5 studies only.


Geographic view of C25: LMIC countries tend to have higher OA shares. Reachability mirrors evidence production patterns.





M7 — Where Evidence Is Youngest


<span class="figure-badge badge-atlas">Atlas</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-map-growth.R</span>


Share of studies since 2018 by country. Countries with ≥5 studies only.


Recent growth concentrated in specific regions — shows where the field is expanding geographically.





M8 — Dominant Evaluation Method


<span class="figure-badge badge-atlas">Atlas</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-map-method.R</span>


Cost-utility North / cost-effectiveness South. Countries with ≥5 studies only.


Geographic manifestation of C11/C8: HIC = CUA (QALY), LMIC = CEA (natural units). The metric divide is spatial.





M9 — Disease Atlas (11 Small Multiples)


<span class="figure-badge badge-atlas">Atlas</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-map-disease.R</span>


11 small-multiple maps, one per GBD Level-1 cause group. Shades absolute study counts (log). Disease contrast is the point, not absolute peak.


Infectious diseases light up Africa/South Asia; NCDs light up HIC regions; injuries diffuse. The spatial disease signature of HEE research.

title: Act V — Gaps vs Burden (The GBD Climax)
text:
The map’s whole point. Variables: study counts × GBD DALYs (country total + 22 Level-2 causes) × income, via crosswalk_mesh_gbd.csv.




C21 — Evidence per Unit of Burden, by Country


<span class="figure-badge badge-hero">★★★ Hero</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-burden-mismatch.R</span>


Log–log scatter: studies ÷ DALYs × income. The 18× gap between high- and low-income medians.


18× gap in evidence per DALY (HIC median vs LIC median). Within-group spread 50–141× dwarfs between-group 12.9×. The central GBD finding.





C22 — Research Share vs Burden Share, by Disease


<span class="figure-badge badge-hero">★★★ Hero</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-burden-disease.R</span>


Dumbbell plot: research ÷ burden ratio, LMIC vs HIC, by GBD Level-2 cause.


Maternal-neonatal: 3.6× burden share in HIC vs 0.37× in LMIC. Injuries: 0.21× in LMIC. Cardiovascular, neurological also starkly mismatched. The disease-level gap map.





C23 — Largest Absolute Evidence Deficits


<span class="figure-badge badge-hero">★★★ Hero</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-deficit.R</span>


Ranked deficit bars: studies vs burden-expected. Where is the MOST missing evidence in absolute terms?


India +4,847 studies short; Nigeria +1,205; Indonesia +920; Pakistan +780; Bangladesh +620. Absolute deficits concentrate in populous LMICs.





C24 — High Burden, Low Research (Injustice Plot)


<span class="figure-badge badge-hero">★★★ Hero</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-injustice.R</span>


Burden × evidence plane + burden-proportional diagonal, bubble size = population. Which settings have high burden AND low research AND low income?


Editorial closer: bottom-right quadrant = high burden, low evidence, large population, low income. Nigeria, DRC, Ethiopia, Tanzania, Uganda cluster here.





C30 — Within-LMIC Inequality (Lorenz)


<span class="figure-badge badge-hero">★★★ Hero</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-inequality.R</span>


Lorenz curve of LMIC evidence vs LMIC burden. Is the gap only rich-vs-poor, or steep among the poor too?


Least-served half of LMIC burden holds 16% of evidence; top 5 = 55%. Gini = 0.50. Inequality WITHIN LMICs is extreme — not just HIC vs LIC.





C29 — Epidemiological-Transition Shift


<span class="figure-badge badge-hero">★★★ Hero</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-transition.R</span>


LMIC research disease-mix (3 transition classes) over 2010–2026 vs 2021 burden. Research shifted communicable→NCD past burden shares; injuries stuck.


Communicable 68%→28%, NCDs 31%→70% (2010→2025). Injuries ~1% throughout vs 11% burden — the transition bypassed injuries entirely.





T4 — Method Streamgraph Over Time


<span class="figure-badge badge-timeline">Timeline</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-method-stream.R</span>


Econ-eval-type composition over time (2010–2025). Cost-utility 45%→54%, cost-effectiveness 34%→25%.


Field increasingly adopts cost-utility (QALY) methods; cost-effectiveness declining. Method shift mirrors metric shift in C11/T2.

title: Act III — Methods & Quality
text:
What gets measured, and how well? Variables: 14 outcome families, uses_qaly, econ_eval_type, design_basis, model_based; abstract text for C14.




C10 — Outcome Families


<span class="figure-badge badge-solid">★★ Solid</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-outcome.R (exploratory)</span>


14 outcome families, direct-labelled bar. What kinds of benefit are counted?


QALYs, survival/mortality, and clinical events dominate. “Unspecified benefit” catch-all reveals reporting quality gaps.





C11 — The Comparable-Metric Currency


<span class="figure-badge badge-hero">★★★ Hero</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-metric.R</span>


QALY vs DALY use by income group, grouped bars. The metric flips by income.


QALYs for rich, DALYs for poor — cross-income comparability is broken. HIC: ~55% QALY, ~5% DALY. LMIC: ~35% QALY, ~25% DALY. No common currency across the income divide.





C12 — Model vs Measurement Over 17 Years


<span class="figure-badge badge-hero">★★★ Hero</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-model-over-time.R</span>


model_based × year × income. Is the field drifting to modelled (vs measured) evidence?


Model-based share rising across all income groups; LMIC model-dependency higher than HIC at every time point. Field increasingly relies on decision models, not trial-based evidence.





C13 — Source → Analysis → Outcome (Alluvial)


<span class="figure-badge badge-hero">★★★ Hero</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-alluvial.R</span>


Alluvial diagram: design_basis → econ_eval_type → outcome family. How evidence flows from design to method to benefit.


RCTs flow heavily to cost-utility/QALY; observational designs spread across types; model-based studies dominate cost-utility pathway.





C14 — Decision-Framing in the Abstract


<span class="figure-badge badge-hero">★★★ Hero</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-decision.R</span>


Grouped bar (4 elements × All/HIC/LMIC): ICER, threshold, uncertainty (PSA), perspective. Abstract-only proxy — “not reported ≠ not done”.


Most abstracts report NONE of these. ICER 39%, threshold 22%, PSA 28%, perspective 31%. LMIC reports them slightly MORE often than HIC, not less. Honest stand-in for blocked reference-case audit.





T5 — Decision-Usefulness Over Time


<span class="figure-badge badge-timeline">Timeline</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-decision-time.R</span>


Share of abstracts foregrounding each decision-analytic element by year (2010–2025). Temporal companion to C14.


All four rose: threshold most (12%→29%), ICER (25%→48%), PSA (15%→38%), perspective (18%→42%). Reporting improving but majority still foregrounds none.





3.5 — Method–Outcome Mismatch (Lancet)


<span class="figure-badge badge-paper">Paper Figure</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-forest-predictors.R (exploratory)</span>


Heat map: econ_eval_type × outcome family. Do methods report the outcome their definition requires? (CUA without QALY = mismatch).


~9.5% of CUAs report no QALY outcome. Mismatch reveals extraction noise floor (different model calls for type vs outcomes).

title: Act I — The Shape of a Field
text:
How much research is there, and what kind? Variables: year, econ_eval_type, full_eval_status.




C1 — Corpus Hero Board


<span class="figure-badge badge-hero">★★★ Hero</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-statboard.R</span>


Eight stat tiles summarizing the entire corpus in one glance: 38,199 evaluations · 168 countries · 2,845 journals · 94% full evaluation · 46% QALY · 56% model-based · 68% single-country.


Opener figure — sets the scale for everything that follows.





C2 — The Growth Streamgraph


<span class="figure-badge badge-hero">★★★ Hero</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-growth.R</span>


Stacked streamgraph of evaluation types by year (2010–2025), with 2026 flagged as partial. Shows the field’s expansion and shifting composition.


Cost-utility grew from ~40% to ~55% share; cost-effectiveness declined from ~35% to ~25%. The field is growing AND shifting toward preference-weighted metrics.





C3 — Cumulative Growth vs Early Rate


<span class="figure-badge badge-solid">★★ Solid</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-growth.R</span>


Cumulative publication line with early-rate reference line and half-since-2020 marker. Tests whether growth is accelerating.


More than half of all HEE studies published since 2020 — growth is accelerating, not just continuing.

Radial bar / donut showing CUA 43% · CEA 29% · CCA 17% · CBA 5% · others. Folds into C2 streamgraph; kept for quick reference.

<span class="figure-badge badge-hero">★★★ Hero</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-disease.R</span>


MeSH C-tree circular bar, coloured by LMIC/HIC lean. Shows which disease areas dominate and whether they skew rich or poor.


Infectious diseases lean LMIC; neoplasms, cardiovascular, musculoskeletal lean HIC. The lean is visible in the colour gradient.





C8 — Disease × Evaluation Method


<span class="figure-badge badge-solid">★★ Solid</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-disease-method.R</span>


Heat map: for each GBD disease group, the mix of economic-evaluation types. Rows with ≥300 studies.


Cancers and chronic conditions lean cost-utility (QALYs); injuries and maternal-neonatal care lean cost-effectiveness (natural units).





C31 — Thematic Landscape by Income (UMAP)


<span class="figure-badge badge-hero">★★★ Hero</span>
<span class="figure-script">05-topic-model.py + R/fig-companion-topicmap-income.R</span>


Emergent topic map (embeddings → UMAP → HDBSCAN) coloured by each theme’s LMIC share. Protocol Appendix K.


Theme-space segregates: LMIC themes = malaria 91%, TB 66%, HIV 57%, maternal 57%; HIC themes = obesity 3%, dementia 6%, arthroplasty 10%.





C32 — Emergent Themes Ranked by Income


<span class="figure-badge badge-hero">★★★ Hero</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-theme-rank.R</span>


Horizontal bar: 15 most- + 15 least-LMIC themes, coloured by share, faceted. Lancet-friendly league table of C31.


The two ends don’t overlap: LMIC themes 33–91%, HIC themes 3–13%. Research about poor and rich countries sits in completely different thematic spaces.





C29 — Epidemiological Transition Shift


<span class="figure-badge badge-hero">★★★ Hero</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-transition.R</span>


LMIC research disease-mix (3 transition classes) over 2010–2026 vs 2021 burden. Communicable → NCD shift tracked against burden shares.


Research shifted communicable 68%→28% to NCDs 31%→70% (2010→2025), crossing burden shares. Injuries stayed ~1% throughout vs 11% burden.

title: Act IV — Geography & Authorship
text:
Where is the research about, and who produces it? Variables: country (190), income, UN region, multi_country; affiliation country + institution. Extracted-geo only for income comparisons (audit finding 17).




C15 — Global Proportional-Symbol Map


<span class="figure-badge badge-hero">★★★ Hero</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-dotmap.R</span>


Berrang-Ford style dot map: country counts, bubbles by income, Robinson projection. Where is the evidence on a map?


Evidence concentrated in North America, Western Europe, East Asia. Africa and South Asia visible but sparse. Dot size = study count, colour = income.





C16 — Density Within & Between Income Groups


<span class="figure-badge badge-hero">★★★ Hero</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-burden-mismatch.R (paper fig 3)</span>


Studies per capita × income, dot strip. Is the gap between income groups, or within them?


Both: between-group gap is large (17.8× median), but within-group spread (50–141×) dwarfs between-group spread. Some LMICs outperform many HICs.





C17 — Top Producers: Volume vs Per-Capita


<span class="figure-badge badge-solid">★★ Solid</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-top-producers.R</span>


Two-rank slope chart (log axis): who leads by count vs by output per person.


USA/UK/China lead by volume; small wealthy countries (Netherlands, Sweden, Switzerland) lead per-capita. Different leaders for different metrics.





C18 — Who Leads Research About Each Setting


<span class="figure-badge badge-hero">★★★ Hero</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-authorship-pattern.R</span>


Stacked bars: local only / local+foreign / foreign only, by income group of country studied. Extracted geography only.


28% of low-income country studies have NO local author. Foreign-only dominates LIC; HIC research is mostly local. Parachute research visible in the data.





C19 — Income-Group Collaboration Structure (Chord)


<span class="figure-badge badge-solid">★★ Solid</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-collab.R</span>


Chord diagram: cross-income co-authorship of 32,731 eligible studies. Self-loops (within-group) excluded from ribbons.


High-income teams are the hub. 24,162 wholly HIC studies vs 37 wholly LIC. Every income group connects mainly through HIC. Cross-income collaboration is HIC-mediated.





T1 — Equity Over Time


<span class="figure-badge badge-timeline">Timeline</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-equity-time.R</span>


LMIC share of annual single-country output vs their burden share (2010–2025). Is research attention shifting toward need?


Rose 16% → 36% (2010→2025) — real progress, yet still far below 83% LMIC burden share (dashed line). Shaded band = distance to burden-proportional reference.





T2 — QALY-Metric Convergence by Income


<span class="figure-badge badge-timeline">Timeline</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-qaly-time.R</span>


QALY use by income group over time. The metric gap over time.


LMIC 15% → 49% vs HIC 51% → 59% (2010→2025). Gap narrowed ~10pp but persists. LMIC catching up on comparable metric adoption.





T3 — Reach Over Time


<span class="figure-badge badge-timeline">Timeline</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-reach-time.R</span>


Cumulative % of each income group’s countries with ≥1 evaluation. Country universe denominators per income group.


HIC covered early; LIC reached last (28% → 96%). Geographic reach expanding but uneven — LIC coverage only recently approaching saturation.

title: Act VI — Bibliometrics
text:
How the evidence is packaged and reached. All harvest-dependent (Wave 0 emit). Reflexively ties back to the full-text-access limitation.




C25 — Open Access Over Time & by Income


<span class="figure-badge badge-solid">★★ Solid</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-openaccess.R</span>


is_oa × year × income, lines. 93% base (after DOI supplement harvest). Is the evidence reachable — and is reachability equal?


OA rose 46% → 80% (2010–2024). LMIC research more open than HIC at every year. Mirrors the full-text-retrieval limitation we face.




C26 — Language of the Evidence


<span class="figure-badge badge-thin">★ Dropped — Null</span>
<span class="figure-script">—</span>


Corpus is 99.8% English, flat across regions. A one-line limitation, not a figure. The English-database search systematically misses non-English HEE literature.


Dropped — null finding. Non-English HEE is absent from the map; absence concentrated in under-served regions.




C27 — Where It Is Published (Journal Concentration)


<span class="figure-badge badge-thin">★ Thin</span>
<span class="figure-script">🛠️ To build</span>


Journal Lorenz curve / top-20 bar. How concentrated is the literature across journals? (Harvest 93% base, journal 87.5% coverage).


Thin unless concentration is striking. Buildable now on harvest data.




C28 — Who Funds It (Funder Landscape)


<span class="figure-badge badge-thin">★ Thin</span>
<span class="figure-script">🛠️ To build</span>


Top funders bar from funders field (~28% coverage, as-harvested). NIHR/HTA/NIH/MRC variants lightly merged — a floor, not a census.


Thin: caption the base honestly. Funder pack F5 is the richer version of this.

title: Funder Decision Pack (F1–F5)
text:
Built for a funder (Wellcome) asking: “Where does the next pound buy the most missing evidence, and where would I just duplicate what the field will produce anyway?” These lean to ranked tables/quadrants a committee can act on rather than maps.

Honest limits: No cost or research-funding-amount data → ranks by gap, never by cost-to-close or value-for-money. F5’s funders field ~28% coverage (floor, not census). “Proportionality to burden is a reference point, not a target” throughout.





F1 — Opportunity Matrix: Disease × Income


<span class="figure-badge badge-funder">Funder Pack</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-funder-opportunity.R</span>


Each cell = disease group’s share of research ÷ share of burden within that income level. Red = under-researched (opportunity), blue = over. Grey cells <15 studies = gap can’t even be measured.


Deep red cells — injuries, maternal-neonatal, cardiovascular in lower-income settings — are where research is most absent relative to burden. Low-income cells too thin to measure. The “WHERE × WHAT” decision tool.





F2 — Priority Scorecard


<span class="figure-badge badge-funder">Funder Pack</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-funder-scorecard.R</span>


Burden × intensity scatter + ranked deficit bar. The shortlist for investment.


India +4,847 studies short, Nigeria +1,205, Indonesia +920, Pakistan +780, Bangladesh +620. Ranked absolute deficits — the actionable shortlist.





F3 — Capacity-Building Quadrant


<span class="figure-badge badge-funder">Funder Pack</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-funder-capacity.R</span>


Burden × local-authorship share. High-burden, <75%-local set = fund people, not just studies.


DR Congo, Ukraine, Ethiopia, Tanzania, Uganda — high burden, low local authorship. Fund capacity (researchers, institutions), not just individual studies.





F4 — Self-Correcting vs Stuck


<span class="figure-badge badge-funder">Funder Pack</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-funder-trajectory.R</span>


LMIC research-to-burden ratio: era-1 (2010–2017) → era-2 (2018–2026). Arrows right = closing gap; stuck left = funding additional.


Injuries, cardiovascular, neurological, maternal — stuck below burden share and NOT closing (injuries/maternal worsening). These are where funding is most additional. Infectious diseases closing on their own.





F5 — Funder Landscape


<span class="figure-badge badge-funder">Funder Pack</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-funder-funders.R</span>


Top funders by studies, split by income. Who pays? Be additional.


Most big funders are HIC-focused; Gates dominates LMIC; Wellcome has a real LMIC share. ~28% coverage — know the base. Fund where others aren’t.

title: Lancet Paper Figures
text:
The tight, ~10 journal figures for the paper submission. Greyscale-safe, descriptive titles, legends present, uncertainty shown.

Core set (VISUALIZATION_PLAN.md): 3.1 cascade · 4.2 density · 4.4 transition · 4.3 disease×income · 4.5 authorship · 5.1 coverage curve · 5.2 burden scatter (GBD) · 6.1 predictors forest · 3.5 method–outcome mismatch · plus PRISMA.





Figure 1 — PRISMA Flow Diagram


<span class="figure-badge badge-paper">Paper Core</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-prisma.R (to build)</span>


Standard PRISMA: 115,405 records → 44,941 extracted → 38,199 eligible full evaluations.





Figure 2 (3.1) — Decision-Usefulness Cascade


<span class="figure-badge badge-paper">Paper Core</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-cascade.R</span>


Funnel: all records → extracted → eligible → full eval → model-based → QALY → decision-framing. Faceted by income.


Each rung narrows; LMIC survives at higher rates through early rungs but drops at decision-framing. The cascade argument in one figure.





Figure 3 (4.2) — Evidence Density Within & Between Income


<span class="figure-badge badge-paper">Paper Core</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-burden-mismatch.R (density panel)</span>


Dot strip: studies per 10M population × income group (4-level). Within-group spread vs between-group gap.


Within-group spread (50–141×) dwarfs between-group (12.9×). Some LMICs outperform many HICs. The “indistinguishable” claim was an income-miscoding artefact (fixed).





Figure 4 (4.4) — Epidemiological Transition Trend


<span class="figure-badge badge-paper">Paper Core</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-transition.R (Lancet finish)</span>


Slope: disease mix by income × era (2010–2017 vs 2018–2026). Communicable → NCD shift vs burden shares.


LMIC research shifted communicable→NCD past burden shares; injuries stayed ~1% vs 11% burden. The transition bypassed injuries.





Figure 5 (4.3) — Disease Composition by Income


<span class="figure-badge badge-paper">Paper Core</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-companion-disease.R (Lancet finish)</span>


Heat map: MeSH C-tree disease share × income group (4-level). What diseases dominate where?


Infectious dominates LIC/LMIC; NCDs dominate UMIC/HIC. The disease-income gradient is the baseline for all gap analysis.





Figure 6 (4.5) — In-Country Authorship by Income


<span class="figure-badge badge-paper">Paper Core</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-authorship-pattern.R (Lancet finish)</span>


Point + CI: local author share × income group. Extracted geography only.


Local authorship drops sharply with income: HIC ~85%, LIC ~30%. 28% of LIC studies have NO local author. Parachute research quantified.





Figure 7 (5.1) — Coverage Curve (Lorenz)


<span class="figure-badge badge-paper">Paper Core</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-coverage-curve.R</span>


Cumulative studies vs cumulative population (Lorenz-style). Coverage is broad but shallow.


Top 20% of countries (by population) hold ~80% of studies. Broad geographic coverage, but shallow depth.





Figure 8 (5.2) — Burden Mismatch Scatter (GBD)


<span class="figure-badge badge-paper">Paper Core</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-burden-mismatch.R</span>


Log–log scatter: studies ÷ DALYs × income. The 22× gap. GBD 2023 all-cause DALYs.


22× gap in evidence per DALY (HIC vs LIC median). Within-group spread dwarfs between-group. The central GBD finding for the paper.




Figure 9 (6.1) — Predictors Forest Plot


<span class="figure-badge badge-paper">Paper Core</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-forest-predictors.R (to build)</span>


Coefficient / odds-ratio forest: what predicts generic metric use? (income + design + model + disease + year). Shared figure for 6.1–6.3.


To build: logistic regression of uses_qaly ~ income + design_basis + model_based + disease + year. Strongest Lancet figure — turns descriptive gaps into structural drivers.




Figure 10 (3.5) — Method–Outcome Mismatch


<span class="figure-badge badge-paper">Paper Core</span>
<span class="figure-script">R/fig-forest-predictors.R (exploratory)</span>


Heat map: econ_eval_type × outcome family. CUA without QALY = mismatch (~9.5% of CUAs). Extraction noise floor (different model calls).


Methods don’t always match their definitional outcome requirements. The noise floor for any method–outcome claim.
